title: Divine Motherhood of Mary (Theotokos)
summary: The Blessed Virgin Mary is truly the Mother of God (Theotokos) because she conceived and gave birth to Jesus Christ, who is one divine Person with two natures, divine and human; this dogma, defined at Ephesus (431), safeguards both Christ's divinity and the unity of his Person.

blocks.text: Introduction: The Dignity of the Mother of God

The dogma of Mary's divine motherhood is the foundation of all Marian doctrine and devotion. Because Mary is the Mother of God, she possesses a dignity infinitely surpassing all other creatures. This truth is not primarily about Mary, but about Christ: it safeguards the unity of his Person and the reality of the Incarnation. [CCC 495, 509]

The title Theotokos, meaning God-bearer or Mother of God, was solemnly defined by the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus in 431. This definition was not an innovation but the clarification of what the Church had always believed: that the one born of Mary is truly God made man. [CCC 466, 495]
And why is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?

blocks.title: CCC 495: Mother of God
blocks.text: Mary is truly the Mother of God because she conceived and gave birth to Jesus Christ, who is one divine Person, true God and true man, in the unity of his Person.
I. Biblical Foundations of Divine Motherhood

The New Testament clearly teaches that Mary conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit and gave birth to the Son of God. The angel Gabriel announced that the child to be born would be called holy, the Son of God. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, proclaimed Mary as the mother of my Lord. [CCC 488, 495]

St. Paul writes that God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law. St. John's Gospel proclaims that the Word became flesh, implying that the one born of Mary is the eternal Word made man. These texts affirm that Mary's son is divine. [CCC 488, 495]
And the angel said to her, The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God.

blocks.title: CCC 488: Born of the Son of God
blocks.text: Scripture affirms that Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit and gave birth to the Son of God; the one born of her is the eternal Word made flesh, truly divine.
II. The Council of Ephesus (431): Definition of Theotokos

The Nestorian heresy claimed that Christ was two persons, one divine and one human, and that Mary was only the mother of the human person (Christotokos), not the divine. The Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus condemned this error and defined that Mary is Theotokos, God-bearer, because the one born of her is one divine Person. [CCC 466]

The Council proclaimed: If anyone does not confess that the Emmanuel is truly God and therefore that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God (Theotokos), let him be anathema. This definition safeguards the unity of Christ's Person: Mary bore not a human person loosely united to God, but the Person who is God. [CCC 466, 495]
But when the time had fully come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law.

blocks.title: Ephesus (431): Theotokos Defined
blocks.text: Ephesus defined Mary as Theotokos, condemning Nestorianism; Mary bore one divine Person, not a human person separate from the Son of God.
III. The Hypostatic Union and Divine Motherhood

The dogma of Theotokos is inseparable from the doctrine of the hypostatic union—the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one divine Person. Because there is only one subject in Christ, the eternal Son, Mary is the mother of that one subject, who is God. [CCC 466-467, 495]

Mary did not give birth to a nature but to a Person. She conceived and bore the Person of the Son of God, who assumed a human nature from her. Therefore, she is truly the Mother of God, not merely the mother of Christ's humanity. [CCC 495]
And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.

blocks.title: CCC 495: One Person, Not Nature
blocks.text: Mary bore a Person, not a nature; she conceived the one divine Person of the Son, who assumed human nature from her, making her truly the Mother of God.
IV. The Council of Chalcedon (451): Confirmation

The Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon confirmed the teaching of Ephesus, defining that Christ is one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation. The Council reaffirmed that the holy Virgin is Theotokos, since the Word was united to flesh in the womb. [CCC 467]

Chalcedon's Definition confesses one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man, born of the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, according to the manhood. This safeguards both the distinction of natures and the unity of Person. [CCC 467]
Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and designated Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead.

blocks.title: Chalcedon (451): Two Natures, One Person
blocks.text: Chalcedon confirmed Ephesus, defining Christ as one Person in two natures, born of the Virgin Mary, Theotokos, safeguarding both natures and the unity of Person.
V. Theological Implications of Divine Motherhood

Mary's divine motherhood gives her a unique dignity surpassing all angels and saints. She is the highest of all creatures, the Queen of Heaven and Earth. Her motherhood is not merely biological but involves her free cooperation in the work of salvation through faith and obedience. [CCC 509, 966]

Because Mary is the Mother of God, her intercession is powerful and her role in the economy of salvation is unique. She is the New Eve, whose obedience undid the disobedience of the first Eve. Her divine motherhood is the source of all her other privileges and roles. [CCC 411, 494, 511]
For he has regarded the low estate of his handmaiden. For behold, henceforth all generations will call me blessed.

blocks.title: CCC 509: Highest of Creatures
blocks.text: Mary's divine motherhood gives her dignity surpassing all creatures; she is Queen of Heaven, the New Eve, and her intercession flows from this unique role.
VI. Papal Magisterium: Pius XI and Pius XII

Pope Pius XI, in the encyclical Lux Veritatis (1931), commemorated the 15th centenary of Ephesus and reaffirmed the dogma of Theotokos. He emphasized that this doctrine is the foundation of Christology and Mariology, inseparable from the unity of Christ's Person. [Lux Veritatis]

Pope Pius XII, in Munificentissimus Deus (1950), defined the dogma of the Assumption, noting that Mary's bodily glorification flows from her divine motherhood. Because she bore God in her womb, it was fitting that her body be preserved from corruption and assumed into heaven. [Munificentissimus Deus 2]
And he came to her and said, Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you!

blocks.title: Pius XI & XII: Foundation of Mariology
blocks.text: Pius XI reaffirmed Theotokos as foundational to Christology; Pius XII taught that Mary's Assumption flows from her divine motherhood and unique dignity.
VII. Vatican II: Mary in the Mystery of Christ

Vatican Council II, in Lumen Gentium Chapter VIII, placed Marian doctrine within the mystery of Christ and the Church. The Council taught that Mary is truly the Mother of God and of the Redeemer, and that she cooperated in the work of salvation with faith and obedience. [Lumen Gentium 53, 56]

The Council emphasized that Mary's divine motherhood is the source of her unique role in the economy of grace. She is the Mother of the members of Christ, cooperating in the birth and development of divine life in the souls of the faithful. [Lumen Gentium 53, 63]
When Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing near, he said to his mother, Woman, behold, your son! Then he said to the disciple, Behold, your mother!

blocks.title: Vatican II: Mother of God and Church
blocks.text: Vatican II taught that Mary is truly Mother of God and of the Redeemer, cooperating in salvation; she is also Mother of the Church and of the faithful.
VIII. Mary's Cooperation in the Incarnation

Mary's divine motherhood involved her free and active cooperation. At the Annunciation, she gave her fiat, her yes, to God's plan: Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word. Through this act of faith and obedience, she conceived the Son of God. [CCC 490, 504]

The Fathers of the Church contrasted Mary's obedience with Eve's disobedience. As Eve became the mother of all the living in the order of nature, Mary became the mother of all the living in the order of grace. Her cooperation was necessary for the Incarnation to occur. [CCC 411, 494, 511]
And Mary said, Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.

blocks.title: CCC 490, 504: Mary's Fiat
blocks.text: Mary freely cooperated in the Incarnation through her fiat at the Annunciation; her obedience undid Eve's disobedience, making her the New Eve and Mother of all in grace.
IX. Heresies Condemned Regarding Divine Motherhood

The Church has condemned various errors denying Mary's divine motherhood. Nestorianism claimed Mary was only Christotokos (mother of Christ), not Theotokos (mother of God), dividing Christ into two persons. This was condemned at Ephesus (431). [CCC 466]

Modern errors include denying the perpetual virginity of Mary or reducing her role to a mere instrument without free cooperation. The Church continues to affirm that Mary is truly and properly the Mother of God, while remaining ever-virgin and cooperating freely in salvation. [CCC 495, 502]
Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel (which means, God with us).

blocks.title: CCC 466: Nestorianism Condemned
blocks.text: Nestorianism denied Mary is Theotokos, claiming she bore only a human person; Ephesus condemned this, affirming Mary bore one divine Person, true God and true man.
X. Devotion to the Mother of God

Devotion to the Blessed Virgin flows from the dogma of her divine motherhood. The Church honors Mary with the title of Theotokos in the liturgy, especially in the Eucharistic Prayers and the Marian antiphons. This devotion is essentially Christological, leading us to adore her Son. [CCC 971]

The rosary, the Angelus, and Marian feasts all celebrate Mary's divine motherhood. The Church encourages the faithful to invoke Mary as Mother of God, trusting in her powerful intercession. True Marian devotion always leads to deeper love and imitation of Christ. [CCC 971, 2675-2676]

As he said this, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked! But he said, Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!

blocks.title: CCC 971: Christological Devotion
blocks.text: Devotion to Mary flows from her divine motherhood and is essentially Christological; true Marian devotion leads us to adore her Son and imitate his life.
XI. The Perpetual Virginity of the Mother of God

The Church teaches that Mary remained a virgin before, during, and after the birth of Christ. This perpetual virginity is a sign of her total consecration to God and her unique role in the Incarnation. The brethren of Jesus mentioned in Scripture are understood as close relatives, not children of Mary. [CCC 499-501, 507]

Mary's virginity signifies that God alone is the Father of Jesus in his divinity, and that the Incarnation is entirely God's work. Her virginal motherhood is a mystery of faith, revealing that salvation comes from God, not human power. [CCC 503, 505-506]
And Mary said to the angel, How shall this be, since I have no husband?

blocks.title: CCC 499-501: Perpetual Virginity
blocks.text: Mary remained ever-virgin before, during, and after Christ's birth; her virginity signifies that God alone is the Father of Jesus and the Incarnation is God's work.
XII. Living the Faith in Mary, Mother of God

To honor Mary as Theotokos is to deepen our faith in the Incarnation and the divinity of Christ. We imitate Mary's faith, obedience, and total surrender to God's will. Through her intercession, we grow in union with her Son. [CCC 967, 971]

The feast of the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, is celebrated on January 1st, eight days after Christmas. This placement emphasizes the connection between Christ's birth and Mary's divine motherhood. The Church encourages daily prayer of the rosary and devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary. [CCC 971, 2676]
His mother said to the servants, Do whatever he tells you.

blocks.title: CCC 967: Imitate Mary's Faith
blocks.text: Honoring Mary as Theotokos deepens faith in the Incarnation; we imitate her faith and obedience, seeking her intercession to grow in union with Christ.

blocks.title: Closing Prayer: Hail Mary
blocks.text: Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou amongst women and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen.
